# Kapotajātaka (Ja 42)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kapotajātaka* (Ja 42) is a short birth story in the Pali *Jātaka* collection (PTS J I 241–244) [Fausböll 1877; Hallisey & Hansen]. The narrative frame is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha delivers the discourse regarding a greedy monk (*lolabhikkhu*), noting that the monk's greediness also features in the *Kākajātaka* of the ninth book (*Navanipāta*) [Fausböll 1877]. In the tale of the past, the Bodhisatta is reborn as a pigeon (*pārāpata* / *kapota*), while the covetous monk is reborn as a greedy and deceitful crow who comes to ruin through his inability to heed good advice [Fausböll 1877; Hallisey & Hansen]. The canonical verse begins with the opening words *Yo atthakāmassā* [Fausböll 1877]. Following the Buddha's declaration of the Four Noble Truths, the greedy monk attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) [Fausböll 1877]. Charles Hallisey and Anne Hansen discuss the text as an example of Jātaka narrative sub-ethics where animal protagonists do not reflect specific human social conventions or biological instincts, but provide universal moral lessons about human character [Hallisey & Hansen].
